Cronus was an American brand of handheld electronic stopwatches. The semiconductor maker
[Intersil](intersil.md) introduced it in 1973 with the Cronus 1, one of the first quartz digital
stopwatches advertised to swim coaches. From the late 1970s the watches were made by Cronus
Precision Products, Inc., of Santa Clara, California.[^sw7311][^sw7811] Cronus sold a range
of stopwatches to swimmers and timekeepers through the 1980s. By 1992 the brand was being sold
from the address and telephone number of [Accusplit](accusplit.md), and it last advertised
in 2000.[^sw9210][^st0001]

## History

This section follows the brand through the companies that made and sold it.

### Intersil

The Cronus 1 first appeared in Swimming World in November 1973. Buyers sent the order coupon to
Intersil Incorporated in Santa Clara, and dealers were invited to apply.[^sw7311] Intersil was a
chip company, founded by Jean Hoerni in 1967, that made some of the earliest CMOS watch
circuits.[^wiki] In March 1974 Popular Electronics described Intersil's ICM7045, a stopwatch chip
that drove an eight-digit LED display and timed from 0.01 s to 24 hours on three rechargeable
cells.[^popelec] That specification matches the Cronus 1, but no source found says the Cronus 1
used it. The chip notice gave Intersil's address as Cupertino, while every Cronus advertisement
gave 2000 Martin Avenue, Santa Clara.[^popelec][^sw7411]

Intersil added the cheaper Cronus 2 in November 1974 and the Cronus 3 in September 1975, signing
its advertisements "Cronus (Intersil, Inc.)".[^sw7411][^sw7510] A dealer's advertisement of 1976
stated that Intersil both made the watch and designed the integrated circuit inside it.[^sw7607]

### Distribution in swimming

[Seagull Enterprises](seagull.md) of California called itself the only factory-authorized
Cronus distributor in swimming in 1976, and published a national list of dealers.[^sw7607] In
Canada, Cronus advertisements from 1975 carried the Canadian Amateur Swimming Association's
endorsement.[^sn7503] Seagull stopped distributing Cronus in Canada in 1978, leaving
the trade there to its dealer [Mod International](mod-international.md), but remained a major US
distributor.[^sn7808]

### Cronus Precision Products

From November 1978 Cronus advertisements named the maker as Cronus Precision Products, Inc.,
2895 Northwestern Parkway, Santa Clara.[^sw7811] The last advertisement found that names Intersil
is from 1976, and no source found explains how the brand passed from one company to the
other.[^sw7607] The new company said its watches were made, assembled, tested and serviced in the
United States by "the world's largest and longest established manufacturer of digital timers".[^sw7811]
A 1981 directory of aquatic suppliers lists the company at 2890 Northwestern Parkway, the only
source to give that number.[^st8102] Cronus Precision Products exhibited at the American Swimming
Coaches Association clinic in 1984, and its last advertisement with the Santa Clara telephone
number appeared in May 1985.[^st8408][^sw8505]

### Under Accusplit

In 1992 and 1993 Cronus advertised from 2290A Ringwood Avenue, San Jose, with a dealer line of
1-800-538-9750, while keeping a Cronus Precision Products copyright notice.[^sw9210] The address
and telephone number were those of Accusplit, a competing stopwatch maker.[^st8102][^sw9112] No source found
says that Accusplit owned the brand, but a collector's history records that Cronus Precision
Products later moved to Pleasanton, where Accusplit is now based.[^decode] A 2000 buyers' guide listed
Cronus under the same telephone number as Accusplit, and Cronus advertised itself as "Independent
and Direct", sold only through a factory website. No later advertisement has been found.[^st0001]

## Products

This section lists the Cronus lines in the order they were first advertised. Prices are as
advertised in the United States.

| Model or series | First advertised | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cronus 1 | November 1973 | Quartz; red LED; 0.01 s to 23:59:59.99; four timing modes; rechargeable cells; desk-clock base on the dearer model; $165 or $195[^sw7311][^sw7312] |
| Cronus 2 | November 1974 | Same four modes; 60-minute range; disposable cells; $125[^sw7411] |
| Cronus 3 (3S, 3T) | September 1975 | Single event plus either split (3S) or Taylor lap timing (3T); 59:59.99 range; AA cells; $59.95 by 1976[^sw7510][^sw7607] |
| Olympian | July 1976 | Single-event timer; 60-minute range; low-battery warning; $39.95[^sw7607] |
| Cronus 2-D | July 1976 | Two displays showing cumulative split and lap time together; $125[^sw7607] |
| LC-20D, LC-40CD | February 1978 | Liquid-crystal display, over a year on two AA cells; LC-20D all modes with a 1-2 finish; LC-40CD counts down from 15 or 5 minutes[^sw7802] |
| LC-MST | 1980 | Four memories; "Single Action Logic" takes each split with one press; water-tight; $79.95[^st8005][^st8102] |
| LC-SJ, LC-AJ | 1980 | Split timer ($39.95) and lane timer ($29.95)[^st8102] |
| LCD Professional Series | 1983 | Single Action Logic; five-year warranty by 1984[^sw8305][^st8408] |
| Speedmaster | May 1984 | Recalls up to 15 splits and converts times to speeds[^sw8405] |
| Competitor Series | 1985 | The Stopwatch, The Splitwatch and The Dual Split; Timeclip with a large dual display[^sw8505][^sw8509] |
| C600 range, C602M100D | 1992 | Chronograph stopwatches and a 100-memory dual-split model; three-year warranty[^sw9210] |
| 100 Memory | 1994 | 100 memories with a stroke-rate mode; $34.50 in 1995[^sw9509][^st9707] |

The early advertisements differ on two details of the Cronus 1. The first gives its weight as
seven ounces and calls its two versions Deluxe and Utility; the next month's gives five ounces and
calls them Executive and Sportsman, at the same prices.[^sw7311][^sw7312] By 1979 Cronus offered
fifteen models, including five wrist-worn water-resistant timers, and marked every model with a
low-battery indicator that it presented as its own feature.[^sw7903] The Science Museum in London
holds a Cronus Precision Products single-event stopwatch with a six-digit LED display, which it
dates to about 1976–1979.[^scimus]

## In swim timing

Cronus stopwatches were sold for the two manual jobs in swim timing: lane timing at meets, where
hand times back up or replace an automatic system, and taking splits in training. The Cronus 1 was
marketed as a replacement for a coach's pocketful of mechanical stopwatches, and the Cronus 3 for
its ability to show hundredths that a timer could round to tenths under the rules of the
day.[^sw7311][^sw7510] Later models added functions for coaches: the 2-D's simultaneous split and
lap display, the memory of the LC-MST and Speedmaster, and the stroke-rate mode of the 100
Memory.[^sw7607][^st8005][^sw8405][^st9707]

Cronus competed for this market with [Accusplit](accusplit.md), [Heuer](heuer.md) and
[Siliconix](siliconix.md). Siliconix ran a comparative advertisement in 1978 that criticised the
Cronus 3S for lacking a fail-safe reset and a 1-2 finish function, and a rival maker's 1975
advertisement set the Cronus 1 against the Accusplit III and Heuer 820.[^sw7802][^sw7503] In 1979
Cronus named the AAU and NCAA track championships and the Boston Marathon among the events that had
used its watches for official hand timing.[^sw7903]
